content: Interventions targeting students from various health professions, including medical doctors, dentists, and allied health professionals, have been implemented to address rural health workforce shortages. An evaluation of rural clinical placements lasting 5–9 weeks for rehabilitation students (audiology, occupational therapy, physiotherapy, and speech-language pathology) in northern Ontario revealed that 27% of students who completed one rural placement chose to work in rural or remote areas after graduation. This percentage increased to 64% for those who completed two or more placements. Higher rural self-efficacy is strongly associated with an increased likelihood of remaining in or returning to rural practice, with a 50% increase in intent for every unit increase in self-efficacy. This effect was independent of factors such as sex, rural background, career status, current practice location, specialty choice timing, or gaps between expectations and experiences. The WHO guideline development group (GDG) emphasized the importance of continuity and sustainability in fostering rural self-efficacy. Ensuring adequate support during student placements can mitigate negative experiences and positively impact future intentions for rural practice. Without proper implementation, there is a risk of negative impacts on both students and communities. The balance of effects strongly favors the intervention, despite moderate resource requirements for implementation, such as ensuring good living and learning conditions for trainees and trainers. The inclusion of rural health topics in undergraduate and postgraduate curricula has been shown to improve recruitment and retention of health workers in rural areas. For example, medical graduates from Memorial University in Canada, which incorporates rural components in its curriculum, significantly contribute to the rural doctor supply. Similarly, a rural curriculum course in Australia improved students’ competencies in medicine, surgery, pediatrics, obstetrics, psychiatry, and clinical examination, with rural-track students performing as well as or better than their urban counterparts. Continuing education and professional development programs tailored to rural health workers have demonstrated positive effects on recruitment and retention. For instance, Scotland’s General Practice Rural Fellowship retained 71% of its graduates, while decentralized training programs in Norway addressed professional development gaps, a key factor in retaining primary care doctors. The GDG emphasized the importance of protected time for continuing education and the need for sustainable implementation, which may involve moderate costs. Enhanced scopes of practice in rural and remote areas, along with targeted continuing education, are expected to improve the availability and quality of health services in these regions. The GDG highlighted the positive impact on health equity, as these interventions promote access to competent health workers and high-quality care in underserved areas. Stakeholders widely accept these interventions, with high feasibility scores reported for their implementation. The WHO strongly recommends designing and enabling access to continuing education and professional development programs that meet the needs of rural health workers to support their retention in rural and remote areas.
